title: Git Time Travel: Finding History in Git
summary: A dense study-notes carousel covering every tool Git gives you to answer 'when and why did this change happen?' — bisect, blame, log searching, pickaxe, and reflog recovery.

chapters.title: 1. The Mental Model: Reading Git History
points: A commit is an immutable snapshot + parent pointer(s) + author/committer + message — history is just a directed acyclic graph
git log defaults to walking commits reachable from HEAD, newest first, via parent links
Author vs committer: author wrote the change, committer applied it (differs after cherry-pick/rebase)
History is NOT the same as reflog: branches are editable labels, reflog is where HEAD actually moved
Key question to ask before choosing a tool: 'which commit introduced X?' vs 'who wrote line Y?' vs 'where did this content go?'
git log --oneline --graph --all as the everyday map-viewing command
Commits are content-addressed by SHA-1 of their data — same change = different SHA (timestamps/parents differ)
Tool cheat-sheet preview: bisect finds bad commits, blame finds line origin, -S finds content changes, reflog recovers anything

chapters.title: 2. git log Searching: Messages, Diffs, and Authors
points: git log --grep='regex' filters by commit message (use --all to search every branch)
Combine --grep with --author, --since/--until, --pathspec: git log --since=2024-01 -- path/file.c
-i makes grep/author matching case-insensitive; multiple --grep with --all-match = AND, default is OR
git log -p shows the full patch per commit; -<n> limits count, --stat summarizes files touched
git log -G'<regex>' shows commits whose diff adds/removes lines matching the regex (regex-driven diff search)
-G vs pickaxe preview: -G matches on the diff text, -S matches on occurrence count change — covered in ch. 5
git log -L :funcname:file or -L start,end:file traces the full evolution of a function or line range
git log --follow follows a file across renames (rename detection needed, per-file only)
git log -S/string/ quick inline pickaxe: commits where the count of 'string' changed
git log --format / --pretty to control output; %h %an %ad %s for compact archaeology lines
Performance tip: pathspec and --since first shrink the candidate set before expensive -G/-S run

chapters.title: 3. git blame: Who Touched This Line?
points: git blame <file> annotates each line with commit SHA, author, date, and line content
-L 10,25 restricts blame to a line range; -L :funcname blames just one function
Each line shows the LAST commit that changed it — not the commit that originally authored the idea
Reformat-only commits pollute blame: find the real change with blame -w (ignore whitespace), -C (detect moved/copied lines from other files), -M (detect moved lines within the file)
blame is O(lines × history) — on huge long-lived files it walks many commits; range-limit with <rev>..HEAD to blame only recent history
git log -p -L on a line range is often clearer than blame for understanding evolution, not just origin
Ignore noisy commits with a .git-blame-ignore-revs file (supported by GitHub and git blame --ignore-rev) — list mass reformat commits by SHA
--porcelain or git blame --line-porcelain for machine-readable output in scripts/editors
GUI extras: vscode 'Toggle Blame Annotations', GitHub 'Blame' view shows blame-per-line with side diffs
Gotcha: blame follows the current file path by default — renamed files need --follow or blame the old path
Worked example: suspect line -> git blame -w -C -> copy SHA -> git show <sha> to see the full commit in context

chapters.title: 4. git bisect: Binary Search for the Broken Commit
points: Bisect is a binary search over commit history: O(log n) steps to find one bad commit among n
Basic flow: git bisect start; git bisect bad [commit]; git bisect good <known-good-commit>
Git checks out the midpoint commit each round; you test, then mark git bisect good/bad until one commit remains
Automate: git bisect run <command> — command exit code 0 = good, non-zero = bad (125 = skip this commit)
Example: git bisect start HEAD v1.0 then git bisect run make test — fully unattended search
git bisect skip handles commits that can't be tested (won't build); results may become approximate
git bisect log saves the session; replay it later with git bisect replay <file>
git bisect visualize / git bisect view opens a log/graph of remaining candidates mid-search
Always git bisect reset when done — otherwise you're stuck on a detached HEAD at the culprit
Bad test = bad bisect: flaky tests or environment drift make bisection lie; verify the culprit with git show
Works on any measurable property with good/bad semantics — perf regressions (bad = slower) too, not just bugs

chapters.title: 5. Pickaxe: -S and -G Content Archaeology
points: git log -S'string' (pickaxe) lists commits where the NUMBER of occurrences of 'string' changed (added or removed)
git log -G'regex' lists commits whose diff contains added/removed lines matching the regex
Key difference: -S counts occurrences across the whole diff; -G matches per changed line — -S finds 'string appeared/disappeared', -G finds 'line matching pattern changed'
-S takes a literal string by default (use --pickaxe-regex to treat it as a regex); -G always takes a regex
Classic use: find when an API was renamed — git log -S'oldFunctionName' --oneline shows both introduction and removal commits
Pair with --pickaxe-all to show commits where ANY file (not just the matching one) changed the count
Combine with pathspec: git log -S'timeout=30' -- config/ narrows to where the default changed
To find what changed FOR a line, take the SHA from pickaxe and run git show <sha> -- <file>
Pickaxe is faster than -G generally (string count vs regex) but less precise for pattern matching
It searches full history by default — add --since or a range like v1.0..HEAD to bound the cost
Gotcha: a commit that changes surrounding lines but keeps the string count identical is invisible to -S (use -G instead)

chapters.title: 6. Reflog: Recovering 'Lost' Commits
points: git reflog records every move of HEAD (and each ref with git reflog <ref>): commits, resets, rebases, checkouts — default 90 days, 30 for unreachable
'Deleted' commits stay alive as long as a reflog entry references them — nothing is truly lost until gc prunes reflog entries
Recover a botched reset/rebase: git reflog, find the pre-disaster entry, git reset --hard HEAD@{n} or git checkout -b rescue <sha>
HEAD@{n} = n moves ago; HEAD@{'2 hours ago'} = time-based; branch@{n} is that branch's own reflog
Restore a deleted branch: find its last SHA in git reflog, then git branch <name> <sha> — instant resurrection
git fsck --lost-found finds dangling commits even after reflog expiry — the last-resort recovery tool
Rebase recovery shortcut: the reflog entry 'rebase (start)' points at the original pre-rebase HEAD
Reflog is local-only — it is never pushed; it cannot help recover commits someone else lost on the remote
Accidental hard reset with uncommitted changes: uncommitted work was never in a commit — reflog can't get it back (editor swapfiles/IDE local history can)
Prevention habits: git branch backup-before-rebase, or use --autostash; gc.reflogExpire controls retention

chapters.title: 7. Comparisons, Trade-offs, and Common Mistakes
points: Decision table: 'which commit broke the build?' -> bisect; 'who wrote this line?' -> blame; 'when did this symbol appear?' -> pickaxe -S; 'when did lines matching X change?' -> log -G; 'where did my commit go?' -> reflog
Cost profile: bisect = O(log n) test runs (tests are the expense); blame = full history walk per file; -S/-G = diff scan over every commit in range; log --grep = metadata-only, cheapest
Precision vs speed: --grep (fast, message quality dependent) < -S (fast, count-based) < -G (slower, regex-precise) < blame -C (slow, deepest analysis)
Mistake: blaming the reformat commit and stopping — always check -w, -C, and blame-ignore-revs before accusing the author
Mistake: forgetting git bisect reset, leaving a detached HEAD 'broken' repo
Mistake: bisecting with a flaky or environment-dependent test — reproduce manually at the culprit first
Mistake: confusing HEAD@{n} (reflog, local) with HEAD~n (parent chain, pushed) — they diverge after resets
Mistake: pickaxe without a pathspec or date bound scanning the whole repo history for minutes
Mistake: expecting blame/reflog to survive rebase-and-force-push on a teammate's machine — reflog is per-clone
Habit: alias pl = log --oneline --graph --all, and keep a blame-ignore-revs file for formatting sweeps

chapters.title: 8. Case Study & Summary: A Full Archaeology Session
points: Scenario walkthrough: a customer reports a regression, no one knows when it started — apply the full toolkit in order
Step 1 — reproduce and bound it: write a failing check, git bisect start; bad HEAD, good last-release tag
Step 2 — automate: git bisect run ./repro.sh pins the culprit SHA in ~log2(n) steps
Step 3 — understand it: git show <sha> for the commit, git blame -w -C -L on the affected lines for context
Step 4 — find related history: git log -S'deleted_symbol' to see when the dependency appeared/vanished, git log -p -L for the function's evolution
Step 5 — if the fix needs rebase and it goes wrong: git reflog -> reset --hard HEAD@{n} -> nothing lost
Summary rule: bisect answers WHERE, blame/pickaxe answer WHEN and WHO, log -G/-L answers HOW it evolved, reflog answers WHAT HAPPENED locally
Cheatsheet block: the 6 one-liners worth memorizing (bisect run, blame -w -C, log -S, log -G, log -L, reflog reset)
Prevention: small commits, meaningful messages, tags on releases — every archaeology tool gets sharper on clean history
Final reminder: Git history is append-mostly and reflogged — with these five tools, 'lost' is almost never permanent
